title: Previous Permutation With One Swap
statement:
`arr` is an array of positive integers that may contain repeated values. A **swap** picks two positions `i` and `j` and exchanges `arr[i]` and `arr[j]`.

Among all arrays you can get from `arr` with exactly one swap that are **lexicographically smaller** than `arr` (at the first position where the two arrays differ, the new array holds the smaller value), return the lexicographically largest one. If no single swap makes the array smaller, return `arr` unchanged.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every pair of positions and comparing the results works but costs O(n²) swaps, each compared in O(n). To stay as large as possible, the change should happen as far right as possible. A swap at positions `i < j` makes the array smaller exactly when `arr[j] < arr[i]`, so `i` must have some smaller value to its right. The rightmost such `i` is the rightmost **descent**, where `arr[i] > arr[i + 1]`; everything after it is non-decreasing. At `i` we want the biggest value that is still smaller than `arr[i]`, and if that value repeats, the leftmost copy, because then the larger value `arr[i]` lands at an earlier position, which keeps the result larger.

## Approach

1. Walk `i` leftward from `n - 2` while `arr[i] <= arr[i + 1]`.
2. If `i` falls below 0, the array is non-decreasing and already the smallest: return it.
3. Walk `j` leftward from the end past every value `>= arr[i]`; the suffix is sorted, so `arr[j]` is now the largest value below `arr[i]`.
4. Move `j` left while `arr[j - 1]` equals `arr[j]`, reaching the leftmost copy.
5. Swap `arr[i]` and `arr[j]` and return `arr`.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [3,2,1]`. Starting at `i = 1`, `2 > 1` is a descent, so `i = 1`. `j` starts at 2 and `arr[2] = 1` is already below 2. There is no equal value to its left, so swapping positions 1 and 2 gives `[3,1,2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): `i` and `j` each move left at most `n` times.
- Space: O(1): the swap is done in place.

## Pitfalls

- Choose the rightmost descent, not the first; changing an earlier position loses more.
- With duplicates, swap with the leftmost copy: `[3,1,1,3]` gives `[1,3,1,3]`, not `[1,1,3,3]`.
- Do not swap with a value equal to `arr[i]`; that leaves the array unchanged instead of smaller.
- A sorted (non-decreasing) array, including one of length 1, is returned as it is.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `i` | position of the rightmost descent, the value that moves right |
| `j` | position of the value that moves left: the largest below `arr[i]`, leftmost copy |
| `temp` | holds `arr[i]` during the swap |

narration.14: ...because moving arr[i] less far to the right keeps the result larger.
narration.16: Swap the two values with a temporary variable.
narration.19: Return the largest array that is smaller than the input.
